Quebec Mining Association president and CEO Emmanuelle Toussaint (left) speaks with The Northern Miner’s Western Editor Henry Lazenby at Xplor in Montreal.
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 10, 2026
Quebec’s miners are pressing Ottawa and the province to coordinate environmental reviews and shorten approval timelines to help restore the industry’s competitiveness, Quebec Mining Association President and CEO Emmanuelle Toussaint says.
About two-thirds of the 45 advanced mining projects examined in a recent association study target critical minerals, Toussaint told The Northern Miner last week in Montreal. She wants governments to measure permitting times from the earliest steps, including the work before an application is deemed complete, while maintaining environmental standards.
“It’s quite demanding to go through two separate processes, quite often covering the same thing,” Toussaint said. “We’re talking about water, fish, the habitat for the wildlife.”
Turning that project pipeline into operating mines also requires governments to plan roads, railways and ports alongside mining developments, she says. Better coordination would help ensure projects and the transport links they depend on are ready together, preventing infrastructure from becoming the next bottleneck.

source_document.body:
Nearly 80% of U.S. fleet operators plan major fleet investments over the next six to 12 months, according to Bain & Company ’s 2026 new US Truck Study.
What’s Related
The study, based on a survey of 210 operators, found that 79% expect their fleets to grow over the next 12 months. More than one-third expect growth of 10% or more.
Bain said the jump in demand comes as autonomy takes center stage and Tesla ramps up capacity.
For truck makers, Bain said the takeaway is about having trucks ready to sell. “The lesson from the last upcycle is that availability wins,” the report said.
Fuel efficiency is top factor
Fuel efficiency is the top purchase factor, cited by 45% of operators. Reliability and uptime came in at 42%, followed by total cost of ownership (TCO) at 37%. All three have led purchase decisions for years, but Bain said TCO has grown in importance. Bain said TCO has “jumped to the top spot alongside fuel efficiency” over the last three years.
RELATED: Ranking the Top 50 Trucking Companies in the U.S.
“Reliability, total cost of ownership, fuel efficiency and sustainability have simply become more important,” one U.S. fleet operator told Bain.
Costs are a big reason why. Seventy percent of operators named fuel prices as their top operational challenge. Nearly half said tariffs and trade policy had a moderate or significant impact on their costs over the past year.
Fleets ready to switch brands
No truck maker earned an “excellent” rating for fuel efficiency in the survey. More than one-third of operators said they would switch OEMs to improve their economics. Among the largest fleets, that number rose to 41%.
“Today’s ‘gas math’ puts every OEM’s market share at risk,” Bain said.
Electric and autonomous truck use growing
The study found that 49% of operators believe electric trucks now offer better TCO than diesel, as long as enablers such as charging infrastructure are in place. With those same enablers, 67% said they would be open to buying a Tesla.
Autonomy is also on the radar. Bain found that 73% of operators are evaluating how to use autonomous trucks in their operations.

Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.
The new feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature. That location can then appear in real time to nearby drivers using Waze, with cyclists displayed as moving icons on the road.
As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.
I’ve long maintained that safety – or more accurately, the perception that cycling isn’t safe – is one of the biggest impediments to getting more people onto bikes.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
That’s especially true in the US, where cyclists are often forced to share roads with cars instead of enjoying the kind of widespread separated cycling infrastructure found in many more bike-friendly countries. And when a cyclist and a multi-ton vehicle have to occupy the same space, making sure the driver knows that cyclist is there can make a big difference.
Of course, an icon on Waze isn’t going to magically make cycling safe. It won’t replace protected bike lanes, better road design, slower vehicle speeds, or attentive drivers.
But I can certainly imagine situations where it could help. Riding at night or in poor visibility, approaching a blind curve, or simply traveling on a narrow road where a driver might otherwise come upon a cyclist unexpectedly are all situations where an advance warning could be useful.
The feature is opt-in through Garmin Connect and activates when the cyclist starts an outdoor cycling activity. Garmin says location sharing is temporary and session-based, and that cyclists’ personal information isn’t displayed in Waze. Of course, anyone who uses a personal GPS device has already accepted that their location is shared with Big Tech in exchange for features they value, but at least we know that any personalized info stays within Garmin instead of proliferating even further.
Garmin LiveTrack itself is free for users with compatible Garmin devices and previously allowed cyclists to share their live location, speed, route, and other information with friends and family. I’ve used it myself as a safety feature when venturing off-road and on longer solo journeys. The Waze integration essentially expands that safety net to nearby motorists.
There’s obviously one big limitation: You need to be riding with a compatible Garmin device, and the driver needs to be using Waze.
But with Waze claiming around 200 million users globally and Garmin being one of the biggest names in cycling computers and fitness watches, that’s not exactly a tiny Venn diagram.
Anything that gives drivers another chance to see cyclists before actually seeing them sounds like a win to me.

source_document.body:
Rising fuel prices and freight rates are putting pressure on corporate supply chains, but sharply with different consequences: Higher costs for automakers, a competitive opening for railroads and an unexpected advantage for some U.S. oil refiners.
Comments from seven executives at Ford (NYSE: F ), Union Pacific (NYSE: UNP ), XPO (NYSE: XPO ) and Valero (NYSE: VLO ) during the latest third-quarter earnings season show why transportation inflation is much more than who pays more for diesel. The effect also depends on how far a company ships, which transport networks it controls and whether its competitors face an even steeper freight bill.
At Ford, Chief Financial Officer Sherry Ann House drew a distinction between the cost of moving vehicles and customers’ willingness to buy them.
“Higher fuel prices are impacting our freight and energy costs. But notably, we are not seeing it impact customer demand for trucks and fleet vehicles at this point,” House said on the company’s earnings call.
Chief Executive Jim Farley put the broader cost pressure into dollars. “We currently expect commodities, memory and logistics costs to represent a year-over-year headwind of about $2 billion at Ford.” That estimate combines several expense categories; Farley and House said growth elsewhere in the business, including software services and parts, was helping offset the increases.
For manufacturers, the burden extends beyond delivering finished products. Automotive parts can cross borders repeatedly before final assembly, leaving supply chains exposed to higher fuel costs at multiple stages.
Railroads see an opening as trucking gets more expensive
Union Pacific Chief Executive Jim Vena described the same fuel-price pressure as a potential source of new business.
“Railroads are much more efficient. It costs us way less per ton to move products across the U.S. So when fuel prices go up, it’s naturally an advantage,” Vena told investors on the company’s October 22 earnings call.
Executives at Union Pacific, Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC ) and CSX (NASDAQ: CSX ) said higher fuel costs and a tightening trucking market were helping move freight toward intermodal rail. But that competitive advantage did not eliminate railroads’ own exposure. Union Pacific said fuel prices hurt its third-quarter operating ratio by 140 basis points, as higher revenue coexists with cost pressure.
At less-than-truckload specialist XPO, executives emphasized control over transportation capacity rather than relief from market rates.
Chief Financial Officer Kyle Wismans said the company’s combined fuel, operating expense and supplies category increased 29%, or $66 million, from a year earlier, primarily because of higher fuel prices. Purchased transportation costs rose another $10 million amid increased freight volume and rising truckload rates.
Chief Executive Mario Harik pointed to the company’s effort to bring more hauling in-house. XPO reduced outsourced miles from roughly 25% when that program began to 5.6% in the third quarter, limiting its reliance on outside carriers as rates increased.
Harik said rising truckload rates were lowering the break-even point for insourcing, and the company did not expect to increase its exposure to outsourced miles. The comments suggest that owning and operating capacity can provide a buffer when buying transportation on the open market becomes more expensive.
For refiner Valero, soaring tanker costs were changing the relative attractiveness of crude supplies and export markets.
“The main story right now in the market is freight rates,” Randy Hawkins, vice president of crude and feedstocks supply and trading, said on a post-earnings conference call. Shipping crude from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia cost $30–$35 a barrel, compared with about $5 a year earlier, he said.
Those costs have helped deepen discounts on some heavy crude grades, benefiting Gulf Coast refiners able to source supplies closer to home. Valero Chief Operating Officer Gary Simmons also identified an advantage on the sales side.
“Higher freight rates actually give us an advantage into the typical export markets into Latin America,” Simmons said, explaining that Valero primarily competes with European barrels in those markets.
Why it matters: Executives portrayed freight costs not only as a margin risk, but as a force reshaping where companies buy, how they move goods and which markets they can serve competitively.

Dealer Selling Restored 1957 Bel Air That Hides Just Two Reasons To Make Buyers Walk Away
73 photos
Photo: Drive the Coast on eBay
1957 continues to be one of the most desirable model years in the history of the Bel Air, and this specimen shows exactly why. While the car has already been restored, so it now presents in immaculate condition, I can’t help but admire those beautiful lines, the fantastic cabin, and the chrome that perfectly highlights the gorgeous design of old-school classics.
That’s why I believe this Bel Air won’t remain up for grabs for too long. The dealer selling the car explains the convertible doesn’t need anything, and you can tell this is true by simply checking out the photos in the gallery.
The paint is absolutely amazing, and I feel that the photos don’t do enough justice to this Bel Air. You should probably see it in person to admire this Bel Air from every angle, so call the dealer and do yourselves a favor and go there to see this car with your own eyes.
Photo: Drive the Coast on eBay There is basically no reason to ignore a 1957 Chevrolet Bel Air when it presents in this kind of condition. This isn’t just a beautiful car but also an iconic model that has now become one of the most recognizable in the history of American classics.
The 1957 model year was the last release of the Tri-Five, so it’s naturally a highly desirable collectible that can cost more than you can imagine when checking the right boxes.
While Ford continued to dominate the American car space, the battle was now fiercer than ever, especially as Chevrolet continued to insist on V8 power and luxurious cars. The 1957 Bel Air had both these main focuses, as it wasn’t only a luxurious presence on the road, with a flood of chrome and other exquisite touches exclusive to this top-of-the-line Chevy configuration, but also a more powerful car.
The 1957 model year witnessed the introduction of the 283 Turbo-Fire. If you believe you’ve seen this engine somewhere else, it’s because you had, as this Turbo-Fire ended up making its way to most Chevrolet models produced throughout the ‘60s.
The 283 was based on the 265 that was already available on the Bel Air since earlier in the same decade, but this time, Chevrolet was ready for massive power. It started with a two-barrel configuration and was configured with more powerful setups that included the famous Corvette engines and a fuel-injected variant that produced 283 horsepower when fitted with solid lifters.
Photo: Drive the Coast on eBay A 283 is also installed under the hood of this 1957 Chevrolet Bel Air. The V8 power is exactly what it needed to become a collectible, as a six would have certainly reduced its customer appeal.
I’m pretty sure that you’re looking for those two reasons to walk away that I mentioned in the headline. The car was restored as close to factory specifications as possible, and these two reasons are the exceptions to this ambitious objective.
The aluminum radiator and the electric cooling fan, which, according to the dealer, have been added for “improved drivability,” are the only non-factory-correct parts on this Bel Air. Everything else should align with Chevrolet’s expectations, including the body, the engine, and the chrome.
The Gypsy Red paint looks spotless, and there’s no doubt this is also the case when you have the car in front of your eyes. The vehicle has properly been babied since the moment the restoration was finalized, and there’s absolutely no doubt that this should also be the case once it finds a new home. Parking it in a heated garage is the only way to care for this collectible.
The engine is paired with a 3-speed automatic transmission, and while no additional specifics have been offered, it’s safe to assume that it doesn’t need a single repair. The car should be ready for the road, and if you just want to hop in and drive, you should be able to do this.
Photo: Drive the Coast on eBay Let’s talk money.
I don’t think you need to be a die-hard restoration guy or a Chevrolet fanboy to figure out the price. This is an expensive car, and the frame-off restoration is a sign that you won’t be able to get it for pocket money.
The dealer is selling this car at auction, with the starting bid set at $39,000. However, a reserve is also in place, and that makes perfect sense, as you won’t be able to buy the car this cheap. The dealer did not reveal any information related to the reserve, so it is safe to assume that it’s close to the Buy It Now price configured at $130,000.
This is also the price you have to pay for the car if you want to avoid the digital fight. The auction ends in 4 days, and if you want to see the Bel Air in person, you must pack your bags for a quick trip to Santa Rosa Beach, Florida.

Q2 Metals has delivered the first PEA on its Cisco lithium project in Quebec. Credit: Q2 Metals
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 10, 2026
Q2 Metals (TSXV: QTWO; US-OTC: QUEXF) estimates that developing its Cisco lithium project in Quebec would require $2.93 billion (US$2.11 billion) in initial capital, according to its first preliminary economic assessment (PEA).
The proposed open pit would produce 1.7 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate annually over 28 years, the company reported Tuesday. Cisco is about 600 km north of Ottawa, in Quebec’s Eeyou Istchee James Bay region.
“We are focused on advancing Cisco toward becoming a prominent new source of lithium to meet anticipated future demand around the world,” CEO Alicia Milne said in a release. “Delivery of this PEA marks a major milestone and turning point as we transition from pure exploration to establishing Cisco as a key component of Canada’s broader critical minerals strategy and a major contributor to the local and regional economies.”
The assessment gives Q2 a starting point for weighing construction financing against the deposit’s potential. Its next challenge will be to establish enough geological confidence and engineering detail to support a development decision.
Shares of the company rose 5.6% to $1.70 in Toronto on Tuesday afternoon, valuing the company at about $411 million. They’ve traded between $1.07 and $3.43 over the past year.
Early economics
The PEA estimates after-tax net present value of $13.5 billion at an 8% discount rate and a 39% internal rate of return. It assumes US$1,647 per tonne for concentrate grading 5.5% lithium oxide, before shipping from Quebec.
All-in sustaining costs are estimated at $454 per tonne of concentrate before royalties, on a Quebec port basis.
The May 26 estimate contains 297.4 million inferred tonnes grading 1.36% lithium oxide, containing 4.06 million tonnes of lithium oxide. The assessment relies entirely on inferred resources, which are too uncertain to be classified as mineral reserves.
Q2 had $70.9 million in cash at Aug. 31, up from $16.6 million at February’s end, according to its latest financial filing. It completed a $70-million bought-deal financing in May.
The cash gives Q2 room to fund exploration and study work. The company has no producing assets or operating revenue and acknowledged in the filing that developing mining and processing facilities would require substantial additional funding.
Drilling continues
Q2 extended mineralization 100 metres north in results reported Oct. 7. Hole CS26-096 returned 134.5 metres grading 1.2% lithium oxide from surface. The interval is a drilled length; true width hasn’t been determined.
The company’s work program has combined drilling between existing holes to improve resource confidence with tests beyond the known deposit. Environmental baseline studies and further processing tests are part of that development work.
The deposit is 6.5 km from the paved Billy Diamond Highway, which connects south to Matagami’s rail infrastructure and onward to ports. That access offers a route to customers, although a mine would still need its own infrastructure and approvals.

Xiaomi's Winged SU7 Ultra Prototype Is Back on Track With No Camo Whatsoever
27 photos
Photo: Baldauf
Referred to as either SU7 Ultra Extreme or SU7 Ultra with the Track Package, whatever Xiaomi may be developing at the Nurburgring Nordschleife is certainly going to challenge Porsche's record lap time. Spotted with no camouflage whatsoever, the most track-focused iteration of the full-electric sedan from China displays a ginormous swan neck-style rear wing.
A redesigned front bumper, serious aerodynamic enhancements down the sides, and carbon-fiber componentry are on the menu as well, along with a redesigned aerodynamic diffuser that appears inspired by the world of motorsports. All told, Xiaomi appears to be developing the SU7 Ultra in three directions.
First and foremost, chassis enhancements are critical to lapping the Green Hell faster than the Taycan Turbo GT modified in collaboration with Manthey. Then there's the balance between downforce and aerodynamic efficiency, which needs to be perfectly so in order for this variant of the SU7 Ultra to make sense on public roads as well. The final piece of the puzzle comes in the form of weight savings. And yes, unsprung weight savings are likely as well.
A closer look at the yellow prototype reveals a more prominent front splitter with larger intakes in the bumper, along with two openings in the hood. Those are dual air ducts, and the air they shoot upward creates downforce over the front axle for improved stability when taking a corner at high speed.
The lower section of the front bumper also channels air to the sides, around the front wheels, and Xiaomi also made a case for wheel arch-mounted extractors that would make the 911 GT3 RS blush in awe. Those openings are designed to release high-pressure air trapped inside the front wheel wells, further reducing lift while improving airflow around the front axle.
Photo: Baldauf Look even closer, and you will notice front fenders that curve inward ahead of the front doors. The rear quarters feature cutaways behind the wheels as well, and the side skirts sure mean business. The distinctly motorsport-inspired appearance is topped by the dual-element rear wing.
Impossible to miss, this piece of hardware sits high enough to operate in relatively clean air. The lower section of the wing adds another surface for generating aerodynamic load. Regarding the swan-neck construction, the pylons may hide electric actuators for a drag reduction system.
DRS would be of great help on long straightaways, where less downforce equals higher speeds. The movable section could also change its angle by itself, depending on the drive mode, the governing software, and what the sensors are transmitting to the system's control unit.
Equipped with double-spoke wheels, beefy front and rear brakes, and a carbon-fiber roof that includes a front-facing lidar sensor, the prototype in these photos also features body-hugging bucket seats with a Nurburgring motif on the seatbacks. This alone indicates that Xiaomi wants to dethrone the Manthey-prepped Porsche Taycan Turbo GT at the 'Ring, besting the SU7 Ultra Track Package's previous 7:04 lap time.
The Porker required 6 minutes and 55 seconds with Lars Kern behind the wheel. Vincent Radermecker remains Xiaomi's go-to specialist for Green Hell shenanigans. Including the SU7 Ultra Track Package, the Belgian racing driver broke the four-door sedan record a couple of times with Jaguar's XE SV Project 8. On the second attempt with the V8-powered brute, he lapped the 20.8-km circuit in 7 minutes and 23 seconds.

Juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a new, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core . The new bike keeps much of the moto-inspired styling and performance of the existing Scrambler Hardtail, but trims back several components to knock several hundred dollars off the price.
The new Scrambler Core starts at $1,399 , compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.
Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.
Teens are a major part of the moto-style e-bike market, and Juiced has designed its Scrambler e-bikes as a safer option for those younger riders. In addition to ensuring street-legal performance for most major markets, Juiced rolled out a feature known as Speed Lock, which is essentially a parental control option that lets a parent or guardian set a lower speed limit using a PIN code that prevents their teen from later modifying the speed limit.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The launch comes as part of the rebirth of Juiced Bikes following the brand’s acquisition last year. The company was founded in 2009 and was acquired in 2025 by the co-founders of Lectric Ebikes, who have since brought the brand back with a new generation of its popular Scrambler platform.
Scrambler Core cuts cost without gutting the bike
The biggest changes appear to be in the powertrain, battery, brakes, and suspension.
The standard Scrambler Hardtail launched earlier this year set the standard for the flagship models by using a 750W nominal motor with 90 Nm of torque and reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). Its 52V 19.2Ah battery provides nearly 1 kWh of capacity and a claimed range of up to 60 miles (96 km).
The Scrambler Core steps down to a 500W nominal rear hub motor rated for 1,176W peak and 80 Nm of torque. Top speed is also reduced slightly to 25 mph (40 km/h), while the throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h). Importantly, though, Juiced has retained its 52V architecture, meaning this is still a fairly punchy setup rather than a dramatically detuned budget bike.
Battery capacity takes a hit as well. The standard Core gets a 52V 10Ah battery with 520 Wh of capacity, rated for up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Spending another $200 gets the Core Long-Range with a 52V 15Ah, 780Wh battery and a claimed 60-mile (96 km) maximum range. As with nearly all e-bikes, expect real-world range to fall short of the idealized advertised numbers, which are generally only achievable under the lowest power pedal assist.
Juiced also traded the Talon P4 four-piston hydraulic brakes found on the more expensive Scrambler for Talon P2 two-piston brakes. The KKE inverted fork with 140mm of travel is gone too, replaced by a more conventional aluminum triple-crown fork with 100mm of travel.
Those are meaningful downgrades, but they’re also largely the kinds of changes I’d expect to see when trying to shave $300 off an already competitively priced moto-style e-bike. It’s a strategy we’ve seen play out before in the industry, helping lower costs for riders who want a flagship bike but don’t necessarily want to pay flagship prices.
Even so, important features remain to help maintain the look and feel of the Juiced Scrambler line. The Core still gets 20 x 4-inch fat tires, hydraulic disc brakes, a frame-integrated TFT display, four pedal-assist levels, a headlight, taillight, brake light, and turn signals. It’s a single-speed setup and weighs 73 lb (33 kg), while being rated for a 300 lb (136 kg) payload.
A smaller Scrambler for smaller riders
Perhaps the more interesting addition is the Scrambler Core Midsize.
While the regular Core is recommended for riders 5’2” and taller, the Midsize drops that figure to just 4’10”. Pricing remains the same: $1,399 with the 520Wh battery or $1,599 with the 780Wh long-range pack.
And with an eye towards safety, the Core and Core Mini retain Juiced’s PIN-protected parental speed lock. Parents can set the motor-assisted top speed anywhere from 1-25 mph and lock the setting behind a four-digit PIN. That makes even more sense on the Midsize version, which seems tailor-made for younger riders who want the moto-style look but may not yet comfortably fit the larger Scrambler.
The Core is launching in several decidedly Juiced color names, including Black Nectar, Fruit Punch, Sour Grape, White Grape, Berry Freeze, and Blood Orange, though availability varies between frame sizes and battery configurations. Juiced says preorders are expected to begin shipping around the end of the month.
At $1,399 , the Scrambler Core feels like a logical extension of Juiced’s rebooted lineup. You lose some battery, motor power, braking hardware, suspension travel, and a few mph compared to the Hardtail, but the underlying recipe is largely intact. For riders who mostly want the Scrambler look and feel – or parents shopping for a smaller rider – saving $300 may be a pretty compelling trade. Especially when you consider that the original Juiced Scrambler already led the industry in value for moto-style e-bikes from reputable brands.

Defense manufacturers need to share technical information quickly and securely. A supplier waiting for an approved drawing can hold up production. Sending it through an unmanaged channel can expose sensitive data. Engineering and cybersecurity teams need to address both risks together.
The Pentagon’s suspension of CMMC Phase II requirements has changed the certification outlook. Phase I self-assessment requirements remain in place, as do contractors’ applicable obligations to safeguard defense information.
For defense leaders, protecting engineering data is also a program execution issue. Can authorized teams get the right information when they need it? Can contractors maintain control as that information moves between systems and organizations?
CAD models, technical drawings, requirements, bills of material, manufacturing instructions, and test results can all contain Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). As designs evolve, teams share that information across engineering disciplines, production operations, and supplier networks.
Contractors need to understand those movements to protect sensitive data and keep people working from current, approved information. That requires a shared understanding of engineering workflows and cybersecurity responsibilities.
The CUI problem extends beyond individual systems
An inventory of applications containing CUI is a useful starting point. It does not show every place that information may go.
Consider a technical drawing. An engineer creates it in a CAD system and releases it through product lifecycle management (PLM). Manufacturing and quality teams use it, and a supplier receives it to produce a component. Along the way, people may create exports, downloaded copies, or email attachments that also require protection.
Each copy raises questions about access and revision control. Who can use it? Is it still current? What happens when the design changes? An outdated drawing can lead to rework, while an unmanaged transfer can create a security gap.
These questions become harder to answer across supplier networks. Partners need information to perform their work. Contractors need to control what they share, who receives it, and how updates reach the people affected.
Engineering and cybersecurity teams should be able to answer five questions together:
1. Where is CUI created and maintained? 2. Which systems, people, and partners need access? 3. Where do exports and downloaded copies go? 4. How are access and revisions managed when designs change? 5. What records show how information was accessed or shared?
Cybersecurity teams understand the safeguards required. Engineering teams understand how technical information is created, used, and changed. Together, they can identify gaps that an application inventory alone may miss.
PLM connects data protection with engineering execution
PLM manages information that defense programs depend on, including product definitions, bills of material, configurations, engineering changes, and technical documentation. That information supports work across manufacturing, quality, suppliers, and sustainment.
When product information contains CUI, decisions about access, sharing, and revision control become part of the contractor’s cybersecurity responsibilities.
A well-governed PLM environment can help teams maintain an authoritative product record, manage permissions, preserve revision history, and coordinate approved changes. These capabilities help authorized users work from current information within a controlled environment.
PLM supports broader cybersecurity efforts by connecting data governance with everyday engineering work. Contractors still need the controls, processes, and oversight required across their environment, including wherever information is exported or shared.
Where FedRAMP enters the picture
Moving engineering information to the cloud adds another consideration: the security of the cloud service supporting those workflows.
FedRAMP and CMMC serve different purposes. CMMC assesses how defense contractors protect Federal Contract Information and CUI. FedRAMP provides a standardized approach to assessing and authorizing cloud services used by federal agencies.
For defense contractors, there is also a contractual connection. Where DFARS 252.204-7012 applies, an external cloud provider storing, processing, or transmitting covered defense information must meet security requirements equivalent to the FedRAMP Moderate baseline. The provider must also meet the clause’s additional requirements for incident reporting, evidence preservation, and support for investigation and damage assessment.
Using a FedRAMP-authorized service does not automatically make a contractor CMMC compliant. Contractors remain responsible for their own environment, including how they configure access, manage users, and handle information.
Cloud security therefore belongs in the PLM selection process. Engineering and cybersecurity leaders should evaluate how the service protects product information, which responsibilities remain with the contractor, and how teams and suppliers will collaborate.
PTC’s Windchill+ FedRAMP offering helps defense organizations manage product definitions, configurations, and engineering changes in a cloud-based PLM environment. It gives engineering and cybersecurity leaders a shared basis for evaluating how sensitive product information will be managed, protected, and shared.
Start with one engineering workflow
Contractors can begin with a familiar task, such as releasing a technical drawing to a supplier. Map how the information moves from creation through external exchange.
Engineering and cybersecurity teams should identify the authoritative record, the people and systems involved, and any copies created along the way. Then examine how access is controlled and how design changes reach everyone who needs them.
That review can reveal gaps in protection or revision control. Use the findings to prioritize improvements across other workflows and clarify responsibilities with cloud providers and program partners.
The goal is to protect sensitive information while keeping authorized teams working from current, approved product data. That work supports secure program execution regardless of what happens next with CMMC.

Wife Goes to HS Reunion, Finds Rare 1979 Dodge Magnum GT Survivor for Husband's Magnum Collection
43 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
What’s the grandest Mopar you can think of? It’s not a trick question – literally the most grandeur-inspiring of them all. Fine, let’s just settle for classics – which one is it? Don’t go thinking about Crown Imperials, or Chrysler 300s, or some other Plymouth VIP or Dodge Royal Lancer. It’s actually a Dodge Magnum, because the name says it is. And this guy has one of each model year, with the 1979 GT example being the crown jewel.
In everyday parlance, the word "Magnum"—derived from the Latin term for "great" or "large"—instantly conjures images of excess, potency, and larger-than-life proportions. Consumers most commonly encounter the label on oversized 1.5-liter champagne and wine bottles, indulgent ice cream bars, and king-sized beverages or snacks.
In the realm of ballistics, the designation defines large-caliber firearms and ammunition cartridges, such as the .357 Magnum and .44 Magnum, engineered to pack a far heavier propellant charge than standard rounds.
When Dodge needed a commanding moniker for its new 1978 personal luxury coupe, executives borrowed that high-caliber title to project authority during an era when federal emissions standards were strangling Detroit horsepower. Just as importantly, Dodge needed a sloped, aerodynamic nosecone to keep Richard Petty competitive on NASCAR superspeedways after the 1974 Charger expired.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The Magnum supplemented and replaced the B-body Charger SE, holding the line for two seasons before the downsized J-body Dodge Mirada replaced it in 1980.
Across the North American market, the Dodge Magnum nameplate spanned 2 distinct generations, alongside regional V8 and turbocharged 4-cylinder namesakes marketed in Brazil from 1979 to 1981 and in Mexico from 1981 to 1988. The first domestic generation ran for the 1978 and 1979 model years as the final automobile built on Chrysler's venerable rear-wheel-drive B-body mid-size platform.
Riding on a 114.9-inch wheelbase, it competed in the personal luxury segment as a two-door pillared coupe offered in XE and GT trims.
First-generation buyers paid base factory prices between $5,448 and $6,039, choosing between 318-cubic-inch, 360-CID, and 1978-only 400-cube V8 engines, all paired exclusively with a 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Revived after 25 years for a second domestic generation from 2005 through 2008 on the rear-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive Chrysler LX platform, the Magnum morphed into a five-door station wagon. Offered in SE, SXT, R/T, and SRT8 trims from $22,495 to over $38,000, it packed 2.7-liter and 3.5-liter V6s or 5.7-liter and 6.1-liter Hemi V8s with 4-speed and 5-speed automatics.
After assembling 47,827 units in 1978, Dodge produced 25,367 Magnums for the 1979 model year, bringing the two-year B-body production run to 73,194 cars. Every 1979 model rolled off the Windsor, Ontario, Canada assembly line as a two-door hardtop coupe equipped with the 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission, including 3,704 examples ordered with factory T-top roof panels.
Broken down by trim version, 23,693 cars were standard Magnum XEs, whereas just 1,674 buyers stepped up to the Code A75 Gran Touring (GT) package.
With the 400 big-block V8 dropped for 1979, the standard 135-hp 318 two-barrel V8 powered roughly 17,200 cars, while the optional 360 V8 came in 150-hp two-barrel tune on approximately 5,900 coupes and 195-hp four-barrel Heavy Duty Police specification on 2,226 units, including 583 GTs.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile When new, a well-optioned 1979 Magnum GT 360 carried a sticker price around $8,300, squaring off directly against the Chevrolet Monte Carlo, Pontiac Grand Prix, Ford Thunderbird, Mercury Cougar XR-7, Oldsmobile Cutlass Calais, Buick Regal, and Chrysler Cordoba.
Spotting an untouched example of Chrysler's last B-body is a rare treat today, which is why automotive vlogger Lou Costabile documented Dale Lewis and his unrestored 1979 Dodge Magnum GT at the Chrysler Nationals in Carlisle, Pennsylvania. Dale got the vintage coupe in 2025, after his wife, Karen, tracked it down to complete his six-car Magnum collection, which already included a 1978 Magnum survivor and four second-generation Magnums.
Karen became the hero of the story after attending a high school committee meeting to organize a class reunion, where she reconnected with a former classmate and fellow car enthusiast who happened to own this preserved coupe . Originally delivered new through Trail Dodge in Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota, the car still wears its red dealer emblem on the left side of the trunk lid and displays just 48,599 original miles in the center of its 85-mph speedometer (more to the point, it did so in July, 2026).
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The fender tag decodes the E57 360 V8 (two-barrel), a D36 for the A727 3-speed TorqueFlite transmission, A75 Magnum GT package, DLR4 deluxe red leather low-back bucket seats (Code C55), C16 center console, H51 air conditioning, B41 power front disc brakes, G11 tinted glass, G52 left remote mirror, and J25 3-speed intermittent wipers.
Outside, the Spinnaker White body features color-keyed GT wheel flares, 15x7-inch GT road wheels, retractable clear headlight covers, and worn original pinstripes that Dale refuses to replace. Swinging open the long doors reveals a plush crimson interior where XE badges still sit in the woodgrain door trim, paired with the GT-exclusive engine-turned aluminum dash and console appliques that recall a Pontiac Trans Am.
Between the red leather bucket seats rests the console-mounted shifter, facing a full instrument cluster with oil pressure and alternator gauges, a rear defogger switch, and the original AM/FM stereo radio, while the trunk holds a space-saver spare and a 1979 sales brochure.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Underhood, a time-capsule 1979 engine bay houses the 360 V8, rated at 150 hp and 265 lb-ft of torque. Remarkably, the air cleaner still retains its factory Electronic Spark Control System computer—a Lean Burn module most owners tore off on day two—alongside the first-year diagnostic plug, battery heat shield washer reservoir, and assembly line inspection chalk marks.
Even among the better part of 3,000 Mopars gathered at Carlisle this past summer, Dale counts only no more than seven Magnums on the show field. Never mind highways – he’s never seen another on the road. Once Karen retires, the couple plans to take this comfortable 1979 survivor on a Route 66 road trip.

31 photos
Photo: Ford
The Explorer, which is Ford's best-selling sport utility vehicle in the Dearborn-based manufacturer's home market, has landed in another federal investigation. This time, the Office of Defects Investigation has learned that the seat-mounted side airbags may inflict serious burn injuries upon deployment.
PE26008 is what the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration calls this investigation, which covers a mammoth vehicle population. More specifically, an estimated 1,236,155 examples that FoMoCo produced at its Chicago assembly plant in the state of Illinois for model years 2021 through 2026.
The allegations concern drivers and front passengers who sustained burns during crashes that involved side-airbag deployment. Per the ODI, the injuries typically involved second- or third-degree burns. Complaints also identify law enforcement officers driving Explorer -based Police Interceptor Utility models.
So far, the federal watchdog has received 8 vehicle owner questionnaires and 4 Early Warning Reporting Death and Injury reports. A table provided by the NHTSA counts 11 incidents after removing duplicate submissions, with 10 involving burn injuries. Thankfully for everyone, the agency lists no fatalities.
Unlike side-curtain airbags, those mounted inside the front seats deploy alongside the occupant's torso during specific crashes. These airbags are designed to reduce the risk of injury in scenarios that include side impacts. The NHTSA's preliminary evaluation document fails to explain why the reported side-airbag deployments allegedly produced second- and third-degree burns.
Photo: Ford As things stand now, it would be foolish to put the blame on the inflator, the airbag's fabric, deployment pressure, hot gases, or the position of the occupant relative to the airbag. The agency needs time and more data, hopefully from the Ford Motor Company and the airbag supplier as well, to determine what actually happened and why such burns are possible in the Explorer.
Being a preliminary evaluation, PE26008 should not be confused with a safety recall. The Office of Defects Investigation is understandably investigating right now, specifically the scope, frequency, and safety consequences of the alleged issue. Going forward, the NHTSA could escalate this inquiry.
Through September 2026, the Explorer sold no fewer than 189,210 units in the United States market alone. That's 17.6 percent better compared to the first nine months of 2025, putting the Explorer well ahead of the Bronco Sport and Bronco. Natively rear-wheel drive, the mid-size model is a three-row affair that carries a starting price of $38,680 as of November 2026.
Ford says that combined sales of the Tremor and Platinum increased 59.9 percent, while sales of the lesser Active and ST-Line rose 23.3 percent. Not bad for an aging design. Active is what Ford calls the most affordable specification, which is only available with the 2.3-liter EcoBoost I4.
Tremor customers are presented with either the standard 2.3 or the optional 3.0-liter EcoBoost V6, whereas the ST comes with the 3.0-liter unit by default. Weirdly enough, the luxury-oriented Platinum defaults to the 2.3 instead of the punchier six-cylinder lump.

Cyberbeast Is the Only Cybertruck Variant Still Available To Order, but the Price Will Shock You
66 photos
Photo: Tesla
Days after Musk confirmed the Cybertruck would be killed by mid-2027, Tesla scrapped all trims but the Cyberbeast. Not content with the price hike it operated a few days ago, Tesla raised the price of the Cyberbeast again, this time to $109,990. If you count the price of FSD and other extras, the Cyberbeast is now even more expensive than the Foundation Series equivalent in 2023-2024.
The Cybertruck's demise could have been a simple story of a product being launched, selling poorly, and being retired. The sales numbers have been disappointing, to put it mildly, and Tesla could never justify the high production costs for such a low-production vehicle. However, when you zoom out, you notice that the Cybertruck is a part of a trend that points to Tesla winding down its automotive operations.
The Cybertruck's cancellation comes just months after the Model S and Model X ended their careers with a Signature Edition limited series. The two Tesla flagship models were sacrificed to make way for the Optimus robot production line. The Cybertruck fell victim to the Cybercab, or so Musk wants us to believe. Both are bogus reasons, as neither Optimus nor the Cybercab require more production space.
When Tesla announced that the Model S and Model X would disappear, interest in the two EVs spiked, despite repeated price hikes. The Signature Edition models sold out despite the outrageous $159,420 price . Apparently, Musk believes that this recipe might also work for the Cybertruck.
While there's no confirmed "farewell edition" Cybertruck, its price has been cranked up to Foundation Series levels. At the same time, cheaper variants have been discontinued days after their prices have also been increased. This leaves the Cyberbeast as the only option for those who are still crazy enough to buy a Cybertruck for $109,990.
For the price, there's no FSD package paid upfront ($12,000 until April 2024 and $8,000 afterward), no lifetime Premium Connectivity package, and none of the accessories that came with the Foundation Series Cybertruck. This makes the current Cyberbeast even more expensive than the special edition model. The original did not sell very well, and it's doubtful that it will be any different now.
The fact that Tesla no longer accepts reservations for the AWD and Premium AWD variants appears to confirm my concerns. It is highly unlikely that Tesla will ever deliver the trucks to those who ordered the base model for $59,990 in February. Some reservation holders came to the same conclusion and upgraded their orders to the Premium AWD model for a $20,000 difference. However, the Premium AWD variant has also been discarded.
The Cybertruck has been a disappointment from the day delivery started. The price was twice as high as what Tesla announced in 2019, and the range was a far cry from the 500 miles promised. On top of that, Elon Musk made some questionable political choices, and the Cybertruck was regarded as a symbol of his transformation. Many people avoided buying one or even being seen in one, with catastrophic effects on sales.

Ford Analyzed Model Year 2021 Mustang Mach-E Batteries, Most Retain More Than 90% Battery Health
22 photos
Photo: Ford
According to Dearborn's favorite son, more than 2,000 customers have driven their 2021 model year Mustang Mach-E crossovers beyond 100,000 miles (approximately 160,000 kilometers) while retaining more than 91 percent of their usable capacity. Another group of more than 30 vehicles has crossed 200,000 miles (over 320,000 kilometers), averaging 88 percent battery health.
To come up with these figures, Ford examined more than 36,000 vehicles produced for the 2021 model year. Said zero-emission crossovers were sold to both retail and fleet customers in the United States and Canada. The Dearborn-based automaker says that more than 2 billion miles (3.2 billion kilometers) have been accumulated by said vehicles thus far.
The average ownership period sits at 5.2 years, and the fleet retains an average of 92 percent of its original usable battery capacities. 95 percent of analyzed Mustang Mach-Es fall between 87 and 97 percent battery health, with Ford obtaining this information through aggregated connected vehicle data rather than lab tests.
One David Blenkle has exceeded 400,000 miles (over 640,000 kilometers) on the original battery in his Mustang Mach-E, yet his vehicle is a 2022 model that does not belong to the study's population. Based on Ford's internal validation data, these NCM batteries are designed to last 10 years at the very least, with 90 percent battery health at the 100,000-mile mark.
In the Mustang Mach-E's first model year, the second-largest manufacturer among Detroit's Big Three offered nickel-cobalt-manganese packs with either 68 or 88 kilowatt-hours of usable energy. Their gross capacities are listed at 75.7 and 98.7 kilowatt-hours, respectively.
Photo: Ford Both packs could be had with either two- or all-wheel drive. Only the First Edition and the GT received the larger battery with dual-motor AWD by default. Even with all-wheel drive, the Mustang Mach-E is a rear-biased vehicle. That is properly surprising when you remember that its underlying architecture is derived from the front-biased C2 of the Escape, Bronco Sport, and Maverick.
Ford's recommendations for customers who intend to drive their Mustang Mach-E for years to come are pretty sensible. First and foremost, use Level 2 charging for everyday driving. Reserve fast charging on direct current for situations that require it. Preconditioning the vehicle while it's plugged in also matters, and so does avoiding unnecessary exposure to extreme temperatures.
The Blue Oval claims that its wider battery-electric model lineup for North America averages more than 90 percent battery health at 100,000 miles, although that figure comes from a separate 2026 field data study rather than the analyzed 2021 model year Mustang Mach-E vehicle population. For model year 2027, the zero-emission sport utility vehicle offers either 88 or 91 kilowatt-hours of usable capacity.
Select and Premium trims get the lesser battery, while the GT and Rally use the beefier unit. Ford has also improved the Mustang Mach-E for 2027 with a new front electric drive unit that lowers manufacturing costs while delivering the same performance as the old motor. The big news for MY27, however, is the introduction of the Trail Package .
Only available in combination with the Select eAWD, this package should be viewed as a different take on the Rally, complete with increased front and rear ride heights. Prospective customers in the US are expected to receive their Trails in the first quarter of 2027.

Uber Freight is eliminating approximately 80 positions across several departments as part of an organizational restructuring, even as the logistics technology company continues hiring and expanding its managed transportation business.
The workforce reductions, announced internally Tuesday, represent approximately 1.6% to 1.7% of Uber Freight’s workforce and are aimed at simplifying operations, eliminating overlapping responsibilities and improving organizational efficiency .
In an internal memo obtained by FreightWaves, Uber Freight CEO Rebecca Tinucci said the changes are intended to position the company for future growth.
“Several groups have reviewed their structures to simplify how we operate and strengthen execution,” Tinucci wrote. “As a result, we are eliminating roughly 80 roles across the business today.”
The company said affected employees are receiving severance and transition assistance, with managers conducting individual meetings with those impacted.
“These reductions are about aligning our structure for the future, not a reflection of these colleagues’ hard work,” Tinucci wrote.
Nearly 300 open positions despite layoffs
Despite the workforce reductions, Uber Freight is continuing to expand in several business segments , particularly managed transportation, technology and customer-facing operations.
San Francisco-based Uber Technologies (NYSE: UBER ) operates three platforms: Uber (ride-hailing), Uber Freight (logistics), and Uber Eats (food and goods delivery).
Uber Freight has 290 open positions and hired 55 employees over the past 30 days, according to information provided to FreightWaves.
Much of the hiring is concentrated in Uber Freight’s managed transportation business, which the company has identified as a central component of its long-term growth strategy.
Uber Freight said its managed transportation deal volume has increased 2.5 times year over year, with a strong pipeline of prospective business heading into the first quarter of 2027.
The company has also expanded its client engagement team, which supports customers using Uber Freight’s transportation management system and outsourced logistics services.
Uber Freight recently added 18 employees to that team and has several additional openings.
The company characterized the layoffs as operational adjustments rather than a response to broader freight market conditions.
The restructuring includes reducing management layers, eliminating duplicate responsibilities and shifting certain functions between departments, including operations and marketplace teams.
Uber Freight consolidating offices
Alongside the workforce reductions, Uber Freight is consolidating several office locations to bring employees closer to the broader Uber organization and strengthen collaboration.
The company is relocating employees from its Frisco, Texas, office to an Uber location in Dallas, with the transition expected to take place in early 2027.
Uber Freight has also closed its Tinley Park, Illinois, office and moved employees to Chicago, where they will share space with Uber operations.
The company said the office changes are intended to improve collaboration and support joint commercial opportunities between Uber Freight and its parent company.
In Europe, Uber Freight is reviewing its office in Leusden, Netherlands, as its regional operations expand.
The company indicated that the Leusden location has reached capacity and that the review could result in a move to larger office space. No final decision has been announced.
Focus on efficiency and future growth
The restructuring comes as Uber Freight seeks to streamline its organizational structure while directing additional resources toward higher-growth business segments.
Tinucci also emphasized stronger accountability and performance expectations across the organization.
“Alongside these structural updates, we are focused on setting clearer expectations and holding ourselves accountable to our Principles,” she wrote.
The company indicated that the approximately 80 job reductions represent its currently planned workforce adjustments, with no additional rounds announced.
Uber Freight maintains that its managed transportation growth, continued recruitment and investments in customer support demonstrate that the company remains focused on expansion despite the layoffs.
“Making adjustments like these is simply part of running a healthy, evolving business and positions us to better support our customers,” Tinucci wrote.
“To support that continued growth, we are actively hiring in high-demand areas, particularly across TM and client-facing support.”
Why it matters: Uber Freight’s reductions highlight how logistics companies are reorganizing their workforces to prioritize growing business segments even as they eliminate positions elsewhere.

Last month, the FDA committed to designing a “fit-for-purpose” framework for regulating rare disease therapies based on patient need and realistically attainable evidence. With the upcoming decision for Capricor’s Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy deramiocel, this paradigm faces its first key test.
In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, losing the ability to walk isn’t the end of the disease. It’s the start of a new fight to keep the use of your arms and hands. I’m 25; I stopped walking years ago, and I’ve recently started developing sores because I can no longer reposition myself in bed.
I’m not a clinician, and I don’t design trials. But I’ve spent my career in biotech evaluating them and I’ve spent my life being measured by them. When a scale like the Performance of the Upper Limb 2.0 (PUL 2.0) records a lost point, I know what that point used to be.
My unique perspective is what the FDA says it wants . On October 14, the agency launched its Rare Disease Framework Initiative and asked for public input on “fit-for-purpose” review based on realistically attainable evidence. The agency’s comment docket is open until Dec. 11. The clearest test of what fit for purpose means arrives first: On Nov. 22, the FDA will decide whether to approve deramiocel, a cell therapy developed by Capricor Therapeutics—for whom I am a consultant—for upper limb function in Duchenne.
Capricor’s Phase 3 HOPE-3 trial randomized 106 patients with Duchenne, most of them non-ambulatory, to receive deramiocel or placebo for 12 months. Under the analysis published in The Lancet in August, deramiocel slowed upper limb decline on PUL 2.0 by 54% compared with placebo, meeting the study’s primary endpoint.
That result is contested, and anyone following this story knows it. The FDA in briefing documents published in July ahead of an advisory committee meeting said the trial did not meet its pre-specified primary and secondary efficacy endpoints. The published result relies on a revised statistical analysis plan, and reviewers and advisory committee members questioned whether it holds up under alternative assumptions about missing data.

These are fair questions. Changes to an analysis plan should draw scrutiny; that’s how the system guards against wishful thinking. But in rare disease, the question can’t stop at whether or not the plan changed. It also has to consider why, and when. In a 106-patient trial of a progressive, heterogeneous disease, missing data and modeling assumptions can swing results in either direction. A revision made for sound statistical reasons before unblinding is a correction. One made after seeing the results is a rescue. A fit-for-purpose framework should require the FDA to say plainly which it believes this is, and why.
How the FDA responds matters well beyond this one drug. When expectations for analysis plans, endpoints or confirmatory evidence shift late in review, investment capital moves to easier diseases, and patients pay for it.
For deramiocel, the longer-term data also point to efficacy on HOPE-3’s primary endpoint. In the 24-month open-label extension study , patients in the trial who received placebo for a year and then switched to deramiocel saw their rate of upper-limb decline slow by 76% compared with their own preceding year. That analysis wasn’t powered or alpha-controlled, and it can’t substitute for a randomized comparison. But consistency across datasets matters when every patient is precious and a second large trial would take years.
The July 29 advisory committee vote should also be read precisely. Panelists voted 9-3 that the evidence presented by Capricor did not establish deramiocel’s effectiveness for Duchenne cardiomyopathy, the indication the biotech had originally sought. The advisors were not asked to vote on the upper limb endpoint but they did touch on it at the meeting, and their discussion was encouraging. Capricor has since refined the indication to upper limb function and submitted a year of data from the OLE study.

That endpoint deserves more weight than it often gets. In Duchenne patients who are non-ambulatory, upper limb function isn’t a surrogate. It is a measurement of whether a patient can feed himself, drive a power chair, use a phone or hold a job. Once those abilities are lost, they don’t come back. In a progressive disease, slowing decline isn’t a consolation prize. It’s what allows patients to hold on to their last bits of independence for longer.
That changes the cost of delay. Requiring another multi-year randomized trial in a population this small means one cohort of patients will lose function they won’t get back while waiting for the result to arrive.
None of this is an argument for the FDA to lower its standards. It is an argument for standards that are explicit and predictable. Rare disease sponsors invest years in small populations, and they need to know the rules before they place those bets.
A fit-for-purpose framework should commit the FDA to three promises:
Agree on analysis plans and approaches to address potential missing data with sponsors early and hold both sides to them.
Explain clearly how the agency will weigh a contested primary analysis against the totality of evidence.
Treat slowing the loss of function as a meaningful outcome in progressive diseases.
The deramiocel decision will illustrate whether the new framework changes how the FDA weighs evidence, or only how it describes it.
I know what it takes to develop these treatments because I work in this industry. I know what’s lost when they don’t arrive because I live with Duchenne. A therapy that slows progression won’t make headlines as a cure. But for me, it could mean more years with the use of my hands, allowing me to feed myself when I go out to eat with my friends—and more easily continue writing advocacy pieces like this one.

The Port of Long Beach is among the ports highlighted in a maritime electrification proposal that calls for electricity to supply at least 35% of international shipping’s final energy demand by 2035, placing shore-power infrastructure at the center of a broader effort to reduce fossil-fuel use.
The “Maritime Electrification Breakthrough Goal,” released today at a climate conference in Ankara, identifies Long Beach alongside Los Angeles, Seattle and Miami as North American examples of extensive shore-power deployment. Those systems supply electricity to docked vessels through high-voltage connections, primarily serving container and cruise berths, according to the document.
Electricity currently accounts for 20% of maritime energy needs.
The announcement came as part of the coalition co-convened in Ankara by Turkey and Australia. The proposal presents existing port infrastructure as a foundation for a larger transition involving battery-powered ships, expanded electricity networks and renewable generation.
The framework comes as the United Nations’ International Maritime Organization’s debates adoption of the Net-Zero Framework, a global policy aimed at driving increased usage of alternative energy on ships, Nov. 23 in London.
For ports such as Long Beach, shore power connects an existing maritime operation—supplying energy to vessels at berth—with the proposed international target.
Electricity delivered to international ships while docked would count toward the goal, alongside electricity used directly aboard vessels.
The target is specific to international shipping’s final energy demand, rather than the number of ships or the share of port equipment electrified. It represents approximately 2 exajoules of electricity against an estimated shipping energy demand of around 10 exajoules.
One exajoule is a massive amount of energy, equivalent to 278 billion kilowatt-hours, or burning 170 million barrels of oil.
Electricity used by terminal equipment, port-related trucks and trains, domestic shipping and renewable-fuel production would fall outside that calculation. But the framework argues that those activities must be planned together because they rely on interconnected infrastructure.
“Ports sit at the intersection of these systems and will be critical energy and implementation nodes for the transition,” the document states.
Coordinating demand across vessels, terminals and landside freight could improve infrastructure use, support investment in grid capacity and renewable generation, and reduce the risk of projects becoming fragmented or underused, according to the proposal.
The framework links electrification to potential health benefits for communities near ports and freight corridors, where transportation-related pollution can create disproportionate exposure. It says replacing fossil-fuel energy with electricity can reduce particulate matter, nitrogen oxides and sulfur oxides, as well as greenhouse gas emissions. The climate benefits depend on how the electricity is generated.
Shore power is one of several routes identified for expanding electricity use. The document also points to battery-electric vessels, particularly on shorter international voyages, and the electrification of cargo-handling equipment. It cites more than 1,600 fully electric and hybrid vessels operating globally, while noting persistent challenges involving charging infrastructure, maintenance and local technical capacity.
Long-haul shipping, however, will still need liquid fuels, according to the framework. Producing renewable alternatives such as green hydrogen and ammonia would create additional demand for renewable electricity, even though that electricity would not count toward the direct-electrification target.
The proposal warns that available technology alone will not deliver the transition. High upfront costs, uncertain demand, electricity-price risks and long infrastructure development timelines can delay projects, as can disagreements over how ports, terminal operators, utilities and shipowners should divide costs and risks.
It calls for long-term commitments to use infrastructure, utility participation, cost-sharing arrangements, public financing and guarantees to make projects more attractive to investors. Public investment could be particularly important in absorbing early-stage risk and drawing in private capital.
The framework also emphasizes workforce development, including support for shipboard and port workers whose jobs could change as new technologies are introduced. Participating organizations would commit to sharing lessons, supporting demonstrations, facilitating access to finance and reviewing progress annually through 2035.
For developing economies, the proposal sees maritime electricity demand as a potential anchor for broader investment in renewable generation and stronger grids. But it cautions that higher financing costs, constrained electricity infrastructure and limited public budgets can make initial projects especially difficult.
The document urges governments to incorporate maritime electrification into national climate plans and support international measures that provide clearer investment signals.
Why it matters: Expanding shore power and vessel charging requires ports, utilities, terminal operators and shipowners to coordinate grid capacity, infrastructure investment and electricity demand. The proposal treats ports as central to that coordination, not simply as places where ships load and unload.

2028 Ford Mustang Cobra Sound Teaser Indicates FPC V8 Engine, Manual Transmission, Cobra R Variant
21 photos
Photo: Ford / edited
The C8-generation Corvette Z06 is the only American series-production model to feature a naturally aspirated flat-plane V8 as of this writing. Come 2027 for model year 2028, the Ford Motor Company will also gift us a free-breathing V8 with a flat-plane crankshaft. Based on FoMoCo's recently posted teaser clip, the Voodoo in the S550-generation Mustang Shelby GT350 is coming back with a vengeance.
Said teaser clip shows the Cobra name, a moniker that first appeared on a Ford-affiliated vehicle in the 1960s with the debut of the Shelby Cobra. A few years after that, the Cobra name was applied to the 428 Cobra Jet V8-powered Fairlane Cobra and Torino Cobra. Speaking of which, the USPTO database shows Ford as the legal entity that owns the Cobra wordmark in the United States market.
Previously believed to be christened Dark Horse Boss after a different wordmark owned by the Dearborn-based automaker, the next iteration of the Cobra is certain to feature a manual option. You can hear that in the teaser clip, where the distinct pause during upshifts indicates a third pedal rather than a torque converter or a dual-clutch arrangement.
Rumored to come exclusively as a fastback, the 2028 model year Cobra may not even be offered with a two-pedal option. The 10R that Ford developed as part of a joint venture with General Motors never saw a high-revving application. For reference, the dual-throttle-body Coyote engine of the GT and Dark Horse doesn't go higher than 7,500 revolutions per minute.
The manual-only Shelby GT350, meanwhile, shoots to 8,250 revolutions per minute. Said maximum engine speed applies to the GT350R as well. Toward the end of the teaser video, the R in COBRA with all caps is highlighted in blue.
It's also stylized differently from the other letters, and this detail alone is enough for me to get all giddy about a potential Cobra R variant. In a similar fashion to the GT350R from a decade ago, it should come with less weight, better aero, and track-focused chassis tuning.
Photo: Ford The old R offered carbon-fiber wheels, stickier Michelin rubber shoes, a larger front splitter, a carbon-fiber rear wing, and MagneRide damping. To keep it light, Ford removed the rear seats and something else. Indeed, the GT350R did not feature standard air con, floor mats, a tire inflator and sealant kit, or an audio system. The Electronics Package restored much of the deleted equipment, including the floor mats.
Hearsay suggests a wider body than you get with the Coyote-powered Dark Horse, bringing the Cobra a little closer to the supercharged Dark Horse SC styling-wise. While Dark Horse SC-rivaling output figures are completely out of the question, the flat-plane V8 of the Cobra should easily surpass the 500 horsepower of the Dark Horse's engine.
Ford claims the S550-generation Shelby GT350 is good for 526 horsepower at 7,500 revolutions per minute and 429 pound-feet (582 Newton-meters) at 4,750 revolutions per minute. By comparison, the Dark Horse makes 500 horsepower at 7,250 revolutions per minute and 418 pound-feet (567 Newton-meters) at 4,900 when you give it 93-octane premium unleaded.
As noted earlier, the only flat-plane naturally aspirated V8 available in a mass-market American model today is the LT6 of the Corvette Z06. The Detroit-based automaker used Ferrari's architecture as inspiration for this bad boy, whose 5.5 liters of displacement makes it the largest NA FPC V8 to ever grace a series-production model.
Priced from $121,800 for model year 2027, the mid-engine supercar from Kentucky revs slightly higher, with Chevrolet advertising 8,600 revolutions per minute. In optimal conditions, the Voodoo's only American rival develops 670 ponies at 8,400 revolutions per minute and 460 pound-feet (624 Newton-meters) at 6,300 revolutions per minute. Toyota Brings the Scion Back to the U.S., Now as the KEI-01 Mini Truck
35 photos
Photo: Toyota
For about 13 years or so in the 2000s and 2010s, American customers enjoyed the blessings, such as they were, of a wacky car brand called Scion. The over a decade of presence of the Toyota offshoot on the local market has not been easy on the company, though, and it went bust in 2016. Well, guess what?
Somewhat unexpectedly, Toyota announced this week the return of the Scion nameplate on American shores, but this time not as something that can be slapped on extremely small cars named iQ, xA, or tC. This time, it brings along an ultra-compact utility truck called the KEI-01.
The vehicle is, in essence, a local interpretation of the famous Japanese kei trucks. It plays in the low-speed vehicle class, meaning it can only travel at a maximum speed of 25 mph (40 kph), and it has some features here and there that are meant to honor the original Scion nameplate.
The mini truck is powered by a positively tiny 660cc three-cylinder engine, tied to a continuously variable transmission and a four-wheel drive system with auto mode and push-button lock.
At the back, the truck features a three-way fold-down cargo bed of undisclosed capabilities, while the front is occupied by an enclosed cabin with heat and air conditioning, large enough to accommodate reclining and sliding seats and interior cargo spaces.
When it comes to size, the KEI-01 is large enough to get the job done, while at the same time being small enough to become as nimble as possible: it stands 11 feet (3.35 meters) long and under five feet (1.5 meters) wide, and it is capable of carrying 600 pounds (272 kg) of cargo.
Toyota didn't go deeper into explaining everything the KEI-01 is capable of, saying it will do so closer to the launch date. Speaking of that, the truck will hit the market in the second half of next year, and it will be manufactured at Toyota’s Indiana Plant. Despite this, though, and the fact that it is meant for the American market, the vehicle will be offered in a right-hand-drive configuration.
Don't expect it to flood the roads in the hands of private owners, as this is an intentionally low-volume niche vehicle, and as such it will be offered at first to fleet customers. If all goes well, the KEI-01 will try to enter other segments as well later on.
Toyota sees the design as being ideal for use in a variety of activities, including urban commercial duties (especially delivery), farm work, campus jack-of-all-trades, and even for fun activities.
Toyota's mini truck is not the only vehicle to have been presented this week under the revived Scion brand. Two concepts have also been presented, the SxS and BKE. They are both meant to preview the potential development direction for the new Scion.
The SxS is really the same concept that was shown during the 2025 SEMA show. A side-by-side meant for off-roading by trade, it is powered by a turbocharged four-cylinder hybrid powertrain that delivers an incredible (for this kind of vehicle) 300 horsepower.
Toyota confirmed that the design will evolve even further, and it does have a solid chance of being produced sometime in the future.
The BKE, on the other hand, is a very strange contraption, a blend between an electric motorcycle and a stand-up scooter whose component parts and capabilities have not yet been disclosed at the time of writing.

BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem named the two Chinese automakers while speaking at the New Economy Forum in Madrid, as first reported by Grande Prêmio .
But there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal. The FIA is also pushing F1 toward the kind of engine an EV maker has the least reason to build.
What the FIA president said
“One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem said of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.
He said he suggested that BYD buy an existing team instead of starting a new one. BYD wasn’t interested in that route. It wants its own team, so Ben Sulayem told the company to come back with a “serious proposal” that shows the project can work.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
He also made it clear that Chinese manufacturers won’t get special treatment. Any bid would go through the same process as other prospective entrants, and the rules won’t be rewritten to suit them. Right now, there’s no expansion process at all: the FIA isn’t actively looking for a 12th team.
Still, Ben Sulayem repeated that he’d like F1’s next newcomer to come from China, pointing to the country’s EV technology and the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.
BYD has been circling F1 all year
This isn’t new for BYD. Back in March, we reported that BYD was exploring a Formula 1 entry , either by buying a team or building one from scratch.
In April, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD had met F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali in Shanghai and that an entry was “something we’re discussing.” By July, the tone had cooled. Li said “the dream is always there, but we don’t have a concrete agenda,” and special advisor Alfredo Altavilla set a clear condition: “We will never participate in Formula 1 just to put a sticker on the side of a car.”
Altavilla said BYD would only consider F1 to the extent its technology can serve the sport.
Geely is the new name here. The group sold 3.02 million vehicles last year and owns Volvo, Polestar, and Lotus, a brand with decades of F1 history. It’s also heading into Canada next year as Chinese automakers push hard into new markets.
The last newcomer, Cadillac, took a long road. The FIA opened an expression-of-interest process in 2023, and GM’s team only joined the grid as the 11th team this season, running Ferrari power until its own power unit arrives. Audi got in the other way, by taking over Sauber.
The engine problem
Here’s where it gets awkward for an EV maker. The 2026 F1 power units split output roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and electric power, with the MGU-K jumping to 350 kW.
The FIA is already walking that back. In June, it agreed to shift the split to 60-40 in favor of combustion for 2027 and 2028. And Ben Sulayem has been pushing for V8 engines running on sustainable fuel with “minor electrification” for the next rules cycle, starting in 2031 at the latest, possibly 2030. Domenicali says F1 should have a package ready to discuss by the end of this year.
So the FIA president wants a Chinese EV maker on the grid, while pushing a rulebook that makes their main strength less relevant.
Electrek’s Take
We like the idea of BYD or Geely in F1. Chinese automakers have the money and the engineers, and they badly need brand prestige outside China. BYD in particular has been on a performance push with Yangwang, and F1 would be the loudest possible way to tell Europe it’s not just a cheap car brand.
But Ben Sulayem’s comments don’t move things much. There’s no entry process, BYD has already turned down his main suggestion, and Geely’s interest is a name dropped at a conference, not a bid.
A Chinese would likely be good for F1 as well. Motorsports are on the rise in China, and that would be the cherry on top in helping popularize the sport in the world’s largest market.
The bigger issue is the engine. Altavilla was clear that BYD isn’t interested in slapping a logo on a car. It wants F1 to showcase its technology, and BYD’s technology is batteries and electric drive. The FIA’s V8 push goes the other way. It’s hard to sell an EV giant on a sport that’s reducing the electric part of the powertrain.
