Ukraine’s foreign minister said he had urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday to accelerate deliveries of interceptors as Russia ramps up attacks on energy infrastructure to break Ukrainian morale during the winter months.
Speaking after talks with Rubio on the sidelines of a G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris, Andrii Sybiha told Reuters he had pressed Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow even as diplomatic efforts to end the war took place in Abu Dhabi.
“We should work on the peace track, but in parallel we should continue to pressure Russia,” he said in an interview.
Sybiha said he had requested additional support for Ukraine’s battered energy grid and more air-defence interceptors, while confirming that U.S. intelligence sharing and military assistance through the Priority Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program remained in place.
“I raised the issue of how we could speed up some supply, how we could find a proper way to maybe front-load something, and how we could try to find additional quantities,” he said.
Not optimistic on Black Sea ceasefire
His remarks come as Kyiv seeks assurances of continued Western military backing while supporting diplomatic efforts to explore limited confidence-building measures with Moscow.
Commenting on the U.S.-mediated talks now underway between Ukrainian and Russian officials in Abu Dhabi, Sybiha said: “Ukraine has serious intentions … We try to use any opportunity to speed up peace efforts and to make peace closer.”
He said Ukraine remained prepared to discuss a range of de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure.
Sybiha said proposals for a Black Sea ceasefire had been conveyed to Russia through intermediaries including Turkey, Egypt and India, but added he was “not so optimistic” about progress and was still awaiting a response from Moscow.
Sybiha says Putin wants to break Ukrainian spirit
Sybiha reiterated Kyiv’s accusations that Russia is deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure ahead of winter.
“[Russian President Vladimir Putin] tries to break our spirit during the winter,” he said.
Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war, now well into its fifth year.
Sybiha was attending a meeting in Paris of foreign ministers from the Group of Seven, which comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, as well as the European Union.
He said the cost of the war would rise significantly in 2027 and expressed hope that Kyiv could secure longer-term financial commitments from its partners by the end of the year.
“We need macrostability,” he said. “For domestic purposes, it keeps the spirit of our people strong when they understand that at least for one to two years we have long-term commitments.”
Sybiha said his family in Kyiv — including three children — like most Ukrainians, often had only a few hours of electricity a day.
“It means no heating, no water, no sanitation, so it’s a big challenge for us,” he added.

Calibrant Energy, a leading provider of on-site energy solutions, on November 10 announced the close of a $145-million debt facility led by Investec for solar and battery storage projects across multiple U.S. power markets. The portfolio includes a 120-MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) serving a hyperscale data center customer in the PJM territory. Citi, Liberty Bank, and Siemens Financial Services also participated in the facility.
Data center operators are looking for ways to get online faster as PJM and federal regulators work through how large power users connect to the grid. Calibrant’s engineered BESS solutions give energy-intensive facilities greater control over how and when they draw power. This flexibility supports faster interconnection timelines and reduces the need for costly grid infrastructure upgrades that would otherwise be passed on to other ratepayers.
“Data center operators are choosing on-site energy storage because it is a fast, reliable, and effective way to get online and operate as responsible grid citizens,” said Phil Martin, CEO of Calibrant Energy. “With this financial close and site mobilization for a hyperscale data center, Calibrant continues to demonstrate that large-load flexibility is not just possible but a commercial reality today.”
Calibrant’s turnkey, zero-capex solutions unlock the path to reliable power that the world’s largest power users need to grow their businesses. “Investec is proud to support Calibrant and Macquarie on this transaction,” said Fred Petit, co-head of Energy & Infrastructure North America at Investec. “We value the opportunity to partner with experienced investors and operators, and to provide financing that advances the energy transition and the critical infrastructure needed to meet growing power demand across the U.S.”
Calibrant Energy now has more than 5.9 GWh of battery storage capacity in operation, in construction, or under exclusive development agreements, including additional sites with the same hyperscale customer. This growth reflects rising demand from large power users for on-site energy solutions that accelerate speed to power while easing strain on the grid. It also reflects customers’ preference for a trusted, experienced partner that can develop, own, and operate these solutions and deliver the power outcomes their business plans depend on.

GE Vernova announced two significant advancements in the development of hydrogen-ready aeroderivative gas turbine solutions, both achieved at its new dedicated hydrogen testing facility at the Global Technology Center in Greenville, South Carolina.
The company on November 10, in an announcement at the COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, said it has officially validated the performance of its LM2500XPRESS aeroderivative gas turbine package for operation on fuel blends containing up to 50% hydrogen in a Dry Low Emission (DLE) configuration and has successfully completed testing of its LM6000VELOX aeroderivative gas turbine package in a Singular Annular Combustion (SAC) configuration to validate its 100% hydrogen capability.
Building on this legacy of innovation, GE Vernova has now surpassed 11 million operating hours on hydrogen and hydrogen-blended fuels across its global gas turbine fleet. As a world leader in gas turbine fuel flexibility—with more than 120 gas turbines that have operated or continue to operate on fuels containing hydrogen—the company demonstrates proven, real-world operational reliability.
Once produced, hydrogen can be used as a fuel for power generation. Gas turbines capable of operating on hydrogen can support a range of industrial applications, including steel, refining, and petrochemicals.
As the global energy landscape evolves, the demand for fast, flexible, and more sustainable power has become crucial. Aeroderivative gas turbines provide fast-starting, flexible power generation that helps stabilize electric grids, meet peak demand, and respond to changing system conditions.
These operational characteristics allow for the management of peak demand and grid fluctuations, ensuring a steady supply of power to industrial and municipal operators, including data centers and utilities. By integrating these hydrogen-ready technologies, GE Vernova is providing a bridge for customers to use today’s fuels while preparing their infrastructure for lower-carbon options as the energy transition progresses.
“These milestones represent a crucial step in GE Vernova’s commitment to accelerating the energy transition by providing hydrogen-ready solutions that allow customers to lower carbon emissions while maintaining the rapid-start reliability essential for grid stabilization” said Cecilia Giovannelli, CEO of GE Vernova’s Gas Power Aeroderivative gas turbine business. “By rigorously testing these solutions under real-world conditions and beyond, we are doing more than solving today’s technical challenges; we are engineering more sustainable infrastructure to power modern life in the future. Our mission is to deliver the affordable, reliable energy that communities depend on to thrive, ensuring that health and economic prosperity grow in lockstep with our decarbonization goals.”
Technical Achievements in Hydrogen Combustion
LM2500XPRESS Validation: The LM2500XPRESS, a highly flexible, modular package derived from aviation technology, has been successfully validated for up to 50% hydrogen blending in a Dry Low Emission (DLE) configuration. This provides operators with a scalable path to reduce CO2 emissions while retaining the unit’s ability to reach full power in five minutes or less. With more than 1150 units sold and more than 200 million operating hours, the LM2500 remains one of the world’s most widely adopted gas turbines, supporting mission-critical applications ranging from industrial cogeneration and district heating to data centers and grid support.
LM6000 100% Hydrogen Testing: In parallel, the LM6000 platform has been successfully tested using advanced Single Annular Combustor (SAC) systems to validate its capability to operate on 100% hydrogen. This achievement is the result of rigorous engineering mitigating the unique challenges of hydrogen combustion, ensuring stable, reliable operation. GE Vernova has an installed and shipped base of nearly 1,350 LM6000 gas turbine units operating across approximately 60 countries.
Expanding Global Testing Capabilities: The completion of the Aeroderivative testing facility, part of the broader investment in Greenville facility announced in 2025, marks a crucial step in the realization of the company’s strategic commitment to US manufacturing. By establishing this dedicated laboratory, the Global Technology Center has increased its capacity to support the validation of improved product capability such as hydrogen-ready power solutions. This integrated site is now fully equipped to accelerate product testing, enabling GE Vernova to reduce development lead times and provide enhanced support to customers worldwide.
GE Vernova’s hydrogen combustion technology allows power plants to reduce carbon emissions of their existing gas turbines by implementing system modifications which can enable them to run on a wide range of hydrogen concentrations up to ~100% by volume. The retrofitting process involves upgrades for reliable operation.
Beyond aeroderivative solutions, GE Vernova’s hydrogen capabilities also extend to its heavy-duty gas turbine portfolio. The company’s current HA-class gas turbines, including the 7HA and 9HA platforms, can burn up to 50% hydrogen by volume when blended with natural gas using the standard DLN2.6e combustion system. In Türkiye the country’s first H-class gas turbine reached COD in 2026 in collaboration with ENKA.
Global Projects & Testing: Major milestones include hydrogen blend deployments and tests at facilities such as DeBary (USA), NYPA Brentwood (USA), Tallawarra B (Australia), and Guangdong Huizhou (China).

Small modular reactors (SMRs) are emerging as a potentially critical part of the future power mix. Only a year ago, SMRs were still framed as a promising but distant technology. But that’s all changed as electricity demand accelerates, grids struggle to expand at the pace required, and affordability and reliability move back to the top of the energy agenda.
COMMENTARY
What started the year as a trend to watch now looks like a technology tipping into commercial reality—driven less by climate ambition, and more by advancements in industrial artificial intelligence (AI) and the world’s need for more reliable and affordable energy. But the challenge will be not just how to manage the lifecycle of a nuclear power plant from planning through to implementation, but how to deal with its eventual decommissioning.
SMRs are advanced nuclear fission plants that are a fraction of the size of traditional reactors and come without their enormous capital requirements and lengthy development timelines. They are a clean energy source that can be permitted and built far more quickly than a large-scale nuclear power plant.
The conversation has definitely shifted. It’s no longer a question of whether SMRs could play a role, but about where they fit, how quickly they can be deployed, how and what needs to happen to make them commercially viable at scale, including the use of AI. Indeed, in recent IFS research, SMRs were identified by utilities as the second most popular emerging technology for clean baseload power.
While the technology is still emerging, challenges remain, but at the moment, Industrial AI is helping power the move, reliability is reshaping the energy debate, and SMRs are ticking boxes.
What’s Spurring the SMR Drive? Where Sustainability Meets its Match
The energy transition was never about sustainability alone, though this certainly topped the energy and utilities agenda for some time. But in the current market climate, the priorities are reliability and affordability.
While the public likes the idea of sustainability in the abstract, when it collides with a higher bill or an unreliable supply, priorities quickly shift—and in a comfort-driven society, few people are willing to accept real sacrifice to keep sustainability as the top global priority.
For utilities, businesses, and consumers alike, electricity needs to be reliable and affordable. But with the current electrical grid under severe pressure from growing demand, aging infrastructure and geopolitical uncertainty, those priority shifts are becoming increasingly prominent—and it’s exactly where SMRs are stepping in.
SMR Investment Has Gone Global
Every emerging technology follows a familiar arc. It starts out looking like a moonshot—solar power looked exactly this way 10 or 15 years ago, a nice idea that was simply too expensive to take seriously. Then, early adopters step in, and government funding and public capital arrive which de-risk the technology enough for private investment to follow, adoption climbs, and costs come down.
SMRs are now following a similar trajectory. Global government support and early-stage investment are helping to move SMRs from concept toward commercial reality and the market is becoming increasingly international. For example, the UK’s backing of domestic SMR development, alongside growing interest from governments and energy organizations worldwide, is creating momentum that simply did not exist at the same scale a few years ago. The U.S. now treats SMRs as central to its nuclear and renewable power mix, while the European Commission has built them into its Clean Industrial Deal. Canada is widely viewed as an important market to watch as commercial deployment progresses, while China and Russia continue to invest heavily as their own energy requirements grow.
That’s why companies, such as Rolls-Royce, have pushed ahead with their own commercial SMR designs.
The Promise of SMRs—There’s a Lot to Like
As the name suggests, SMRs are made up of smaller, modular units, that offer the potential for a more flexible approach, particularly where a large-scale nuclear facility would be impractical or excessive for the power requirement.
SMRs provide a source of low-carbon power that, unlike renewables, doesn’t rely on the weather for reliable generation. They can be built underground, making them less vulnerable to extreme weather events such as earthquakes, can start up from a completely de-energized state without receiving energy from the grid, and offer great promise for remote regions with less developed infrastructures. This makes them particularly attractive as demand grows from energy-intensive industries and large commercial users.
One of the greatest advantages of SMRs is their potential flexibility. Rather than relying on one enormous generation asset, multiple smaller units could potentially be deployed together to meet the requirements of a large industrial facility, data center or community. The modular design could make it easier to match generation capacity to demand and expand over time, however, it by no means makes the process simple.
SMRs Are Better Together—Demand Barriers Remain
Currently, there are more than 80 SMR designs and concepts globally, and without greater standardization, scaling the technology across borders could become increasingly complex. A collection of SMRs has to function as a coordinated energy system, and it’s where design complexity creeps in.
A collection of SMRs must operate as part of a coordinated energy system. Different manufacturers are in the process of developing various designs, while regulatory requirements can vary by country or region.
A single unit can’t support a data center or major industrial facility on its own, so the model now emerging is a cluster of SMRs operating together as effectively a virtual power plant, aggregated to meet the load of whatever they’re powering.
And barriers go beyond the technology! The challenges are not purely technical. Public confidence in nuclear power with its chequered history of safety, remains a hurdle. Permitting, waste management, supply chains, and site approvals can all add complexity and time to deployment. SMRs may be smaller, but they still operate within the same high-stakes regulatory environment that has historically made nuclear projects complex.
The Real Challenge is Once They’re Switched On—AI Helps Manage the Full Lifecycle
A solution that spans nearly every stage of an SMR’s lifecycle will be essential. Building an SMR is only one part of the equation. The decisions made long before construction begins—around investment, location, capacity and risk—will shape the value and viability of the asset for decades. It’s where Industrial AI can help plan what to invest in, how to size and place it, and building the ROI case as part of a broader asset investment plan. Construction extends into procurement, supply chain coordination, and workforce management for the build itself.
But once they’re switched on, attention will increasingly turn to the technology needed to make them an operational reality. Industrial AI and software must support the development, deployment, and operation by providing unified enterprise asset management, project tracking, and regulatory compliance tools.
Decommissioning is as important as commissioning. Once an SMR is operational, continuous AI-driven monitoring becomes critical—not just for efficiency, but for the public safety assurance regulators and communities demand. And at the end of the asset’s life, that same lifecycle approach carries through to decommissioning and recycling.
From Promise to Power: The Next Chapter for SMRs
The catalysts driving interest in SMRs are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Electricity demand is rising, grid infrastructure is struggling to keep pace, and the pressure to balance sustainability with affordability and reliability is intensifying.
What looked a year ago like a promising but distant technology now looks like something closer to commercially viable—with thanks to industrial AI and forward-looking software. Nuclear may increasingly play a role as organizations balance decarbonization ambitions against the immediate need to keep the lights on, but it’s likely the future energy mix will remain diverse because for SMRs, significant challenges still lie ahead.
— Carol Johnston is VP Industries, Energy, Utilities, and Resources at IFS.

New Hot Wheels Elite 64 Hauler Is a 1979 Chevy C30 Crew Cab Dually 4×4 That Will Cost $65
19 photos
Photo: Hot Wheels Malaysia
I went shopping today and stopped by a few toy stores again. One of them had just brought in the Car Culture: Road Trip mix and I was excited for a moment until I saw the price. They had ramped it up from $9 per piece to $13. Good luck with that! I walked away knowing I could simply get them online for as little as $8 per car.
That might not sound like a big difference, but it can easily add up when you’re buying hundreds of these per year. Also, in hindsight, Road Trip wasn’t all that exciting. I found a new peg-warmer, too, from the Aerostyles mix. And no, it wasn’t the Custom ‘70 Chevy Nova, but the LB-Kaido Works Nissan R32 Skyline GT-R.
Meanwhile, I’m still shaking with excitement knowing that I somehow got my hands on the black 2008 Audi A4 Touring Car: I’ll unbox it for a closer look soon! Until then, I’ve found some new photos of the Premium F1 collection for 2027. We’re moving up to replicas of the 2026 cars and you’ll notice that the card art now features a photo of the driver, too.
That should help with sales, at least for some of the top drivers. I guess this might be your last chance to get your replica of Esteban Ocon ’s F1 machine, as he might not get another chance in the sport. That’s a story for another time, though, as right now I’d like to take you over to Mattel’s Elite 64 series. One of the most highly-anticipated collectibles for the line is just around the corner.
We’ve seen teaser photos and videos for the 1979 Chevy C30 Crew Cab Dually 4x4 for some time, but now is your chance to go after it without having to spend a small fortune. Well, the price is obviously higher than with any other Elite 64 (and even RLC ) release, because the package itself is rather huge for a 1/64th-scale release.
At $65, you get Phil Riehlman’s brand-new Chevrolet C/K truck plus a two-level trailer that can transport up to five cars. The previous two haulers were technically ready to transport six models, although I’ve never had a chance to test that myself. The Freightliner Cascadia originally sold for $50, while the Scania 770 S was slightly more expensive a $55.
Some sellers on eBay will try to charge you as much as $450 for both. I’d suggest trying to get them for less than $150, or aim for other nicer options that aren’t over-hyped. I’m itching for a closer look at some of Ixo’s offerings.
Mini GT and Tarmac Works also have some solutions for that itch, and I guess the best way to go about it would be for me to order a few of them from each brand for a head-to-head comparison.
Anyway, the Duramax Diesel engine under the hood of the C30 is one of the main attraction points, alongside the tire/wheel setup on the rear axle. While I encourage Mattel to bring more pickup trucks to Team Transport, I’d rather Elite 64 Haulers follow the same path as they did for the first two years.
We know for sure that’s how things will be going down in 2027, which is great. The 1979 Chevy C30 Crew Cab Dually 4x4 goes live on Mattel Creations on November 12 2026 at 9 AM PT. Am I the only one who thinks it will be sold out within the first 60 seconds?

ISE BAY, Japan (Feb. 3, 2021) Explosive Ordnance Disposal Technician 3rd Class Benjamin Loell, deployed with Expeditionary Mine Countermeasures Company 1-1 and employed by MCMRON 7, attaches explosives to a prop-mine during Mine Warfare Exercise (MINEX) 1JA 2021. MINEX 1JA is part of an annual series of exercises between the U.S. Navy and the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force designed to increase proficiency in mine countermeasure operations. During the nine-day exercise, participants conduct unit-level mine warfare tactics to include mine hunting, detection, and prosecution. (U.S. Navy Photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Nick Bauer)
In strategic chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz, maritime mines threaten important military assets, shut down commercial traffic or generally cause havoc as transit lanes have to be cleared – and kept cleared – before any traffic can proceed.
The challenge is that it’s easy to mine a body of water and hard to ensure that it’s mine-free. Identifying potential mines, differentiating them from other detritus on the sea floor and neutralizing them is a painstaking, time-consuming process.
“Mines don’t have to be sophisticated,” said Bryan Clark, director of the Hudson Institute’s Center for Defense Concepts and Technology. “There are obviously very sophisticated ones that look for particular acoustic or magnetic signatures. There are some that’ll measure how many ships go across and detonate on the third or fourth ship, but they don’t need to be smart in order to be effective. All you need is somebody to detect the mine and know that it’s there, and it’s going to cause vessel traffic to stop until the mine threat has been eliminated.”
Effectively finding and neutralizing mines has become even harder in recent years, as many nations have retired or pared down their fleets of minesweeping vessels. As the threat of mines increases, however, remote mine hunting capabilities become paramount to ensuring that military, commercial and civilian vessels can safely navigate bodies of water while keeping sailors at standoff distance.
Find, fix and finish
Navies around the world use a tactic known as “find, fix and finish” to neutralize mines. Find is getting a picture of everything on the seabed, ranging from actual mines to junk such as anchors or other material that was disposed of in the water to terrain that looks like a man-made object.
Fix is evaluating everything that was found and eliminating whatever objects can be easily identified as not being mines, then classifying the remaining objects.
“This takes a long time and a lot of dedicated work,” said Mark Bock, vice president for strategy and business development at Advanced Acoustic Concepts (AAC), a Thales company. “Oftentimes it means dwelling on each of those targets one by one. You can imagine how complex this process is in highly trafficked areas such as the Straits of Hormuz.”
Finish is the final step, and it entails identifying mines that need to be neutralized and eliminating them, while protecting against the potential danger of disposing of high explosives.
Crewed and uncrewed systems working in tandem
Traditionally, mine disposal was carried out by minesweeping vessels constructed of wood or fiberglass to avoid creating a magnetic signature, equipped with sonar and other sensor arrays to identify and neutralize mines.
ISE BAY, Japan (Feb. 1, 2021) Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF) and US explosive ordinance disposal technicians, embarked on rigid hull inflatable boats, deploy from the JMSDF Ōsumi-class tank landing ship JS Shimokita (LST 4002) to conduct mine hunting operations during Mine Warfare Exercise (MINEX) 1JA 2023. During the fourteen-day exercise, participants conduct unit-level mine warfare tactics to include mine hunting, detection and prosecution. MINEX 1JA is part of an annual series of exercises between the U.S. Navy and JMSDF designed to increase proficiency in combined mine countermeasure operations and ensure the freedom of maritime navigation. (U.S. Navy Photo by Petty Officer 1st Class Charles Hardmon)
Many of those vessels have been retired, however, including those operated by the US Navy. Now, uncrewed systems are taking the lead in closing the find, fix and finish kill chain, while crewed vessels still play a role.
Towed arrays can be used on either crewed or uncrewed vessels to identify potential mines. The data they collect can be sent to human operators or a system such as an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered classification tool. Using a mixture of crewed and uncrewed vessels helps cover a larger area in a shorter period of time.
Bock gave the example of pairing one or two minesweepers with several robots, allowing for greater coverage than can be provided by crewed vessels alone.
“You can throw a lot more unmanned vessels at a problem than you can manned vessels just from an economic perspective, but also just from a bulk and size perspective,” said Bock. “For instance, the unmanned systems can be put on airplanes and flown into the region, which gives response time and capacity.”
Clark echoed that point, emphasizing that not only are uncrewed vessels cheaper and easier to move, but also can more easily be put on the shelf until they are needed.
“I can buy a lot more robots than I can buy minesweepers, because every minesweeper needs a crew and people are expensive,” he said. “If you want to expand your mine-hunting fleet, you end up having to buy a bunch of manned ships. If you’re buying robots instead, you can buy a bunch of robots, store them, and then bring them out when you need to do the mine-hunting operation.”
Going remote
As previously mentioned, remote systems allow for greater coverage at a lower risk to expensive ships and sailors. But those systems need to be able to identify potential targets and share data with human operators to make decisions on what to engage with and how to engage with it, and that is not a simple task.
“It becomes kind of like a Roomba, where the robots go up and down the route looking for mines in the water column,” said Clark. “They’ll stay near the surface and then look down into the water, and as long as the water is not extremely deep, they’ll be able to see the first 100 or 200 feet of water and detect mine-like objects.”
Effectively identifying a mine – or “not a mine” – is a challenging task in water that can be deep, murky or filled with junk that can mimic the characteristics of a mine.
“The key issue is this huge false-target rate and multiple targets you detect on the bottom – figuring out which ones are man-made and then distilling those down into what are mines,” said Bock. “An old refrigerator thrown onto the ocean bottom is not a mine, but it sometimes is roughly the same size.”
AAC tackles this with an advanced synthetic aperture sonar sensor called SAMDIS. SAMDIS is a multi-aspect imaging sonar that can illuminate targets from multiple angles in a single pass, raising the hit rate on actual targets on an initial sweep. That enables identifying mines on the first sweep through a minefield, allowing for immediate neutralization instead of having to do multiple sweeps to get different perspectives on an object to identify if it is a mine.
Once mines are identified, the company’s Angler neutralization system can eliminate the mines in a less obvious manner than blowing them up and causing a geyser of water that alerts adversaries that mines are being removed.
“The Angler countermine ROV system does not necessarily cause sympathetic detonation,” said Bock. “It will deliver an effect to the mine to neutralize it without the massive explosive reaction.
“Angler also has the capability after delivering the effects to observe the mine or seabed object and document the effects for the operators. In the tool bag of effectors, it’s the only solution today that has semi-covert attributes where the operators are a long way away depending on the scenario from the location of the dastardly deed.”
Future technologies for mine neutralization
While uncrewed systems are taking the lead in mine hunting and neutralization, technology advancements will lead to more efficient, safer mine neutralization in the future.
AI is a key part of that technological advancement, as it enables better pattern recognition, mapping of targets and identifying changes from one sweep to the next.
“By having a clear picture of what’s in the water column, we can do what’s called change detection,” said Bock. “As we tow back through again, the system using AI will find all the things that you knew were there already and haven’t changed in their classification or their location, and also find all the things that are new.”
Clark identified onboard processing and communications as a key technology improvement for remote mine hunting. Instead of the current method of having to download data from mine hunting vessels, then analyzing it, doing another pass to verify potential mines, then sending out other systems for neutralization, being able to streamline that process speeds up the find, fix, finish process.
“If instead you had onboard processing from these mine-hunting vehicles, the underwater vehicles looking for the mines could come up and transmit data back to you immediately and say, ‘I finished path one. I found a bunch of mines or potential mines. They’re here,’” said Clark. “Then you can quickly decide whether to send another vehicle out there right now to investigate, or to just send the mine neutralization system out immediately.
“You should be able to get to a point where you can do this in a way that is just robot after robot after robot.”

Who says long EV road trips mean hours at charging stations? BMW drove the new i3 for over 3 days, covering nearly 3,700 miles, and it took less than 3 hours of charging.
BMW i3 sets efficiency record during long EV road trip
BMW put the i3 to the ultimate test of efficiency, charging speed, and long-distance EV capability on a nearly 3,700-mile Pan-European journey.
The Paneurpeana, as it’s called, is considered the benchmark for range and charging speed. The route begins at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe you can reach by car, and ends in Tarifa, Spain, the southernmost point of mainland Europe.
BMW drove the new i3 50 xDrive for a total of 3,658 miles (5,886.7 km) across eight countries and spent just 2 hours, 45 minutes, and 54 seconds charging at an average of 275 kW.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The performance beat the previous record by more than seven hours, according to Mike Reichelt, head of BMW’s Neue Klasse
BMW said the charging points were not predetermined and that it had to account for external factors such as weather and traffic jams.
(Source: BMW)
The new i3 was impressively efficient during the trip, consuming an average of just 12.5 kWh per 100 km, beating its official WLTP combined energy consumption of 18-13.4 kWh/100 km.
BMW said the trip took 3 days, 2 hours, and 41 minutes, with an average speed of 79.7 km/h, and that the i3 was charged exclusively at public charging points across national charging networks.
The vehicle was driven at all times by a single driver and was not modified in any way, in terms of hardware or software, from the standard i3 available for purchase.
BMW i3 50 xDrive during the road trip (Source: BMW)
BMW’s new i3 uses a 108.7 kWh battery and Gen6 eDrive system that provides a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).
With a drag coefficient of just 0.21, the new i3 is the most aerodynamically efficient BMW vehicle to date.
In the US, BMW said the new 2027 i3 50 xDrive will offer an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 468 miles.
With an 800V architecture, the electric sedan can add nearly 262 miles (423 km) of range (WLTP) in about 10 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds up to 400 kW. In the US, the i3 has a built-in NACS port.
Like the new iX3, the i3 features BMW’s Neue Klasse interior design. The setup consists of BMW’s massive 43″ Panoramic Vision display that spans the base of the windshield and a 17.9″ floating central infotainment display.
The new BMW i3 50 xDrive is on sale in Germany starting at €65,900 with a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).
In the US, the 2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive and 2027 iX3 50 xDrive are available to order , both starting at $61,500.
